note: Nineteen people from the curator's CRDL ledger entries 456-890 who have no record in the database. The pasted ledger held 435 entries but only 287 distinct people; 246 of those already existed under an exact name match and 15 more under a spelling variant. Only these nineteen were absent on both a full-name and a first-plus-surname check against all 8,570 records. Fields follow the house pattern set by the earlier CRDL waves: state Mississippi, era 1960s, Civil Rights ideology, released, arrest date only, and the disposition left explicitly unresolved. Race is never inferred. Gender is set only where the ledger uses a pronoun or a gendered description for that person, and left empty otherwise.

creates.name: Albert Earl Lassiter
creates.description: Albert Earl Lassiter was arrested in Jackson, Mississippi, on March 27, 1961, for the Tougaloo Nine read-in at the whites-only main branch of the Jackson public library, where the students requested service and refused police orders to leave — one of the arrests recorded by the Mississippi State Sovereignty Commission and preserved in the Civil Rights Digital Library, which establishes the arrest and the individual identification photograph. The nine were held roughly thirty-two hours, tried in Jackson municipal court, convicted of disturbing the peace, fined $100 each and given thirty-day suspended jail sentences.

creates.name: Margaret Winonah Beamer
creates.description: Margaret Winonah Beamer was arrested in Jackson, Mississippi, on June 9, 1961, for participating in a Freedom Ride, arrested at the Illinois Central terminal after travelling by train from Nashville with four other riders — one of the arrests recorded by the Mississippi State Sovereignty Commission and preserved in the Civil Rights Digital Library, which establishes the arrest and the individual identification photograph. She was a Central State College student. Accounts outside the CRDL record report that she entered jail on June 11, refused bail and appeal, and remained imprisoned until December 25, 1961 — reportedly the longest full term served by any 1961 Freedom Rider. That chronology is recorded here as reported and needs checking against contemporary court or penitentiary records before it is relied on; it is not entered as custody dates. The disposition, any transfer to the Mississippi State Penitentiary at Parchman, the time served and the release date are not established in the CRDL record and are left unresolved here rather than inferred.

creates.name: Jesse Harris
creates.description: Jesse Harris was arrested in Jackson, Mississippi, on July 6, 1961, for participating in a sit-in against segregation at Livingston Park — one of the arrests recorded by the Mississippi State Sovereignty Commission and preserved in the Civil Rights Digital Library, which establishes the arrest and the individual identification photograph. The arrest photograph is titled Jessie L. Harris while the CRDL authority form is Jesse Harris. He later trained Freedom Summer volunteers and organised in the McComb area and for the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party. A separately catalogued June 2, 1961 Freedom Ride arrest photograph under the name Jesse James Harris may or may not be the same man; the CRDL material does not settle it, so no second record has been created. The disposition, any transfer to the Mississippi State Penitentiary at Parchman, the time served and the release date are not established in the CRDL record and are left unresolved here rather than inferred.

creates.name: James Walker Evans
creates.description: James Walker Evans was arrested in Jackson, Mississippi, on September 13, 1961, as one of fifteen Episcopal clergymen on the Prayer Pilgrimage Freedom Ride who entered the segregated coffee shop and waiting area at the Trailways terminal and refused police orders to leave — one of the arrests recorded by the Mississippi State Sovereignty Commission and preserved in the Civil Rights Digital Library, which establishes the arrest and the individual identification photograph. Most of the fifteen posted bond quickly and continued the pilgrimage; two remained jailed to sustain publicity, and the available account does not identify which two. The arrests later gave rise to Pierson v. Ray. The disposition, any transfer to the Mississippi State Penitentiary at Parchman, the time served and the release date are not established in the CRDL record and are left unresolved here rather than inferred.
